title: Taipei Moves to Jail AI Chip Smugglers as Asian AI Stocks Crack
subhead: Taiwan plans to make unauthorised AI server and chip exports to China a criminal offence carrying five-year prison terms, days after raiding Super Micro's offices. The same week, Asian AI hardware stocks suffered their sharpest slide since July as financing costs, not demand, became the question.

sections.heading: Taiwan Turns Chip Smuggling Into a Felony
sections.body:
Taiwan's government plans to tighten controls on exports of AI servers and advanced semiconductors to Chinese buyers, with unauthorised shipments prosecuted as a crime under the Foreign Trade Act rather than handled as an administrative violation. Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin confirmed the plans in an interview with Bloomberg. Penalties and a start date have not been set.

Until now Taipei relied on a blacklist: Huawei and SMIC have sat on the strategic high-tech goods list since mid-2025, but other Chinese buyers could generally still be served if the goods fell outside the 2022 US export rules. Under the new approach, AI servers and cutting-edge chips would be added to controlled goods across the board, covering all buyers in China. DPP legislator Chung Chia-pin has drafted the amendment to the Foreign Trade Act.

The enforcement record explains the shift. Bloomberg reports Nvidia chips reaching Chinese buyers through smuggling networks in Southeast Asia. Taiwan made its first arrests of suspected AI chip smugglers in May, and in July prosecutors targeted Super Micro managers on forgery charges because existing law had no offence aimed specifically at diverted chips. A raid on Super Micro offices this week sent the company's stock down about 7 per cent, according to Stocktwits.

The timing is tied to Washington. In January Taiwan and the US struck a trade deal cutting US tariffs on most Taiwanese goods from 20 to 15 per cent; in return Taiwanese firms pledged $250 billion of investment in US semiconductors, energy and AI, backed by a further $250 billion in credit guarantees. Taipei is also cashing in: semiconductor exports hit a record $87.2 billion in September, up 60.9 per cent year on year, per Taiwanese trade data cited by Trending Topics.
sections.whyItMatters: Taiwan is converting its role as the world's chip workshop into an enforcement lever. Criminal liability closes the gap that let diverted Nvidia hardware reach China through third countries, and it does so at the point where the physical goods actually leave — which is more enforceable than US rules applied to goods Taiwan sells.

sections.heading: Beijing Answers With Its Own Export List
sections.body:
China's commerce and science ministries have put forward a draft that would restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies, including AI, chip technologies and solar manufacturing know-how, according to AP and Reuters reporting. The proposal extends a list already being expanded: on 16 October, Nikkei Asia reported Beijing was adding AI, biopharma and solar technologies to its export-control catalogue.

SCMP reports analysts see short-term costs but possible long-term gains for Beijing, with a key uncertainty being how open-weight AI models would be treated — something that would matter a great deal for Chinese developers who have built global adoption on open releases.

Neither side has yet responded to the other's move, and neither set of controls is in force.
sections.whyItMatters: Both governments are now restricting outbound technology, not just inbound. China is treating its AI and solar dominance as leverage the way Washington treats lithography — the difference is that Chinese exports of solar equipment and open models are far more embedded in third countries' supply chains, so the collateral damage is wider.

sections.heading: The AI Trade Cracked Where Financing Meets Hardware
sections.body:
Asian AI hardware stocks fell sharply into Monday's open. A Goldman Sachs basket of regional AI hardware names tumbled 11 per cent last week, its steepest drop since mid-July, Bloomberg reported via The Straits Times. US semiconductor shares fell for eight straight sessions — the longest run since 2008 — taking roughly 16 per cent off the sector benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since April 2025.

The winners of 2026 were hit hardest: Nan Ya Plastics, the best performer on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index this year, fell 12 per cent from a record high; Unimicron dropped 14 per cent in a week; Samsung Electro-Mechanics plunged 23 per cent.

The trigger was cost of capital, not demand. Oil surged to $110 a barrel for the first time since May, reviving inflation concerns just as investors focused on the trillions being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave sank to levels signalling distress; its shares fell 12 per cent on 16 October and 25 per cent over the week. Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan has said capital, not memory or fab capacity, will be the binding constraint on AI growth. Gartner warns more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment risk by 2030.

TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix together account for nearly a third of the MSCI Asia ex-Japan Index. Notably, the sell-off continued despite TSMC's upbeat revenue outlook.
sections.whyItMatters: The sector's vulnerability has moved from supply to leverage. Eight of the ten best-performing stocks in the MSCI Asia-Pacific index this year are component makers up at least 236 per cent — a repricing driven by financing conditions rather than any change in chip demand, which is why a TSMC beat did nothing to stop it.

sections.heading: Datacentres Become Battlefield Targets
sections.body:
NBC News reported that datacentres have become targets in active conflicts, with strikes on AI and cloud facilities signalling a new front. Forbes reported separately that Ukraine's widening strike campaign has moved from refineries to datacentres, arguing the shift reveals the limits of attrition-based targeting.

The physical exposure is drawing policy attention in parallel. Hamburg is considering a one-year moratorium on large-scale datacentres, per Buffalo News; Lubbock, Texas has started a datacentre pause while Governor Greg Abbott blocks new permits pending an audit; and Virginia legislators have stacked up moratorium bills ahead of the January session. Public opposition is now a siting risk in the same markets where capacity is being built.
sections.whyItMatters: Compute is now fixed infrastructure in the literal sense — concrete, power contracts and a grid connection that cannot be relocated quickly. That makes it both a military target and a local political one, two risks that did not appear on datacentre business models three years ago.

sections.heading: State Espionage Reaches the AI Labs Themselves
sections.body:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant warned organisations to prepare for wider attacks after the disclosure of a critical flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support software. A suspected China-linked group tracked as Armory Castle used the bug as a zero-day from August, deploying the Sawfly web shell and Bareclaw tunneler for persistence. BeyondTrust shipped updates in October; Reuters reported Google's warning.

The AI race itself is now an espionage target. After a case involving bugging at OpenAI, the White House AI chief described corporate and state espionage as 'realities' of the competition, and former SEC chair Jay Clayton urged US firms and government to be wary of AI-era spying. In Asia, Japanese and South Korean firms have reported mass data exposures — Skyticket (14.64 million records), Burger King Japan (11.18 million), Yamato (5.3 million) — amid what The Straits Times describes as a surge in AI-powered attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: The most valuable assets in the AI economy are model weights, training data and the credentials that reach them — not customer databases. The shift in targeting from consumer data to lab infrastructure is the operational signature of the current phase of the competition.

sections.heading: Launch Capacity Is the New Bottleneck
sections.body:
Blue Origin unveiled a $3 billion Florida expansion to support multiple New Glenn flights per week, with the company seeking to raise its Florida cadence to as many as 50 launches annually (WESH, The Capitolist). New Glenn has been idle since April, and AST SpaceMobile shares fell overnight following a Blue Origin explosion, raising questions about its 45-satellite rollout.

In China, the commercial Zhuque-2 rocket lofted ten satellites in a single launch, with coverage framing it as space computing entering large-scale deployment. Alén Space launched five satellites for Sateliot's 5G non-terrestrial IoT network. India's government published a 'Strengthening India's Space Sovereignty' release, signalling policy attention to launch and orbital capability as sovereign assets.

The commercial satellite market also got a jolt from geopolitics: Eutelsat shares rose about 17 per cent as restrictions on Starlink use in Ukraine drew attention to alternative capacity. Eutelsat said OneWeb is now 15 per cent of total revenue and should reach 22 per cent next year, with growth in Ukraine, aviation and government markets (Space Intel Report).
sections.whyItMatters: Whoever can launch on demand sets the pace for constellations. A single grounded rocket delaying a 45-satellite rollout shows how thin the margin is — and why state-backed launch cadence, not satellite design, is the constraint most governments are now funding.

sections.heading: Greenland Bans Seabed Mining Days After Trump's Announcement
sections.body:
Greenland's parliament unanimously passed a resolution introducing a ban on seabed mineral extraction, one day after US President Donald Trump announced 'massive oil, gas and mineral exploration' would begin on the island, which he described as 'our new and beautiful Greenland' in reference to a September security agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US. RMF24 reported the resolution; Mining.com covered it.

The memorandum stays in force until the end of 2029 with possible two-year extensions, and legislation is expected in the first half of 2027. Greenland holds one of the world's most significant underexplored critical mineral endowments — the Tanbreez deposit carries a 28.2 million tonne TREO resource — and the USGS describes the territory as holding the world's biggest undeveloped rare earth deposits.

Separately, the US has signalled it is nearing approval of deep sea mining permits, and JP Morgan is deepening its critical minerals push, per The National.
sections.whyItMatters: A subnational parliament used its own legislative authority to close a minerals pathway hours after Washington opened one. It is a concrete limit on how far a security agreement translates into extraction rights — and a reminder that critical minerals access runs through local consent, not just great-power deals.

bottomLine: Taiwan's move to criminalise AI chip diversion and Beijing's draft 40-technology export list show both governments now policing outbound flows, not just inbound ones. The more consequential number this week was financial: an 11 per cent weekly drop in Asian AI hardware stocks and CoreWeave bonds trading at distress levels, driven by $110 oil and the cost of debt rather than any weakening in chip demand. The buildout has not slowed, but it is now priced against interest rates. Meanwhile Greenland's unanimous seabed mining ban, hours after Washington announced exploration, shows that critical minerals access is decided as much by local legislatures as by security agreements.
sources: Bloomberg (via The Straits Times, Trending Topics, Investing.com), Reuters, AP, Nikkei Asia, SCMP, Tom's Hardware, Forkast, Startup Fortune, Stocktwits, 24/7 Wall St., OODA Loop, Mining.com, RMF24, WESH, The Capitolist, Space Intel Report, SatellitePro ME, Pulse 2.0, The National, NBC News, Forbes, Buffalo News, Prince William Times, Businesskorea
